text: Does your organisation automatically back up its critical data on a regular schedule?
why: Ransomware can make everyday files unusable. Regular backups help you recover recent work.
recommendation: Set up automatic backups of critical data on a schedule that limits how much work your organisation could lose.

text: Does your organisation follow the 3-2-1 rule: three copies of important data including the working copy, on two types of storage, with one copy kept offsite?
why: Copies stored in different ways and places reduce the chance that one attack or failure destroys every copy.
recommendation: Keep three copies of important data across two types of storage, with at least one copy stored offsite.

text: Does your organisation keep at least one backup disconnected from its systems or locked against changes and deletion so ransomware cannot alter it?
why: Ransomware may attack connected backups as well as working files. An offline or locked backup gives you a protected recovery copy.
recommendation: Keep at least one backup offline or protected against changes and deletion, with access separated from everyday accounts.

text: Does your organisation regularly test restoring critical data from backups and record how long recovery takes?
why: A backup is only useful if you can restore it. Timed tests help you plan for the disruption caused by ransomware.
recommendation: Schedule regular restore tests for critical data and record whether they succeed and how long recovery takes.

text: Does your organisation require a second identity check, such as an approval on a separate device, when signing in to email, remote access and administrator accounts?
why: A stolen password can let attackers enter your systems. A second identity check makes that password harder to misuse.
recommendation: Enable multi-factor authentication for all email, remote access and administrator accounts.

text: Does your organisation give people only the access they need and use separate administrator accounts instead of using them for everyday work?
why: Limited access reduces the damage a compromised account can cause. Separate administrator accounts help keep powerful permissions away from everyday risks.
recommendation: Limit each person's access to their work needs and require separate administrator accounts for system changes.

text: Does your organisation require strong, unique passwords for work accounts, with a password manager available to help staff manage them?
why: Weak or reused passwords can give attackers a way in. A password manager helps staff use a different strong password for each account.
recommendation: Require long, unique passwords for work accounts and provide a password manager to help staff store them safely.

text: Does your organisation promptly remove access when someone leaves and regularly review who still needs access?
why: Unused accounts and old permissions create extra opportunities for attackers to enter or spread ransomware.
recommendation: Assign someone to remove leavers' access promptly and review account permissions on a regular schedule.

text: Does your organisation install security updates for operating systems and software within agreed time limits, with urgent fixes prioritised?
why: Attackers can use known software weaknesses to enter systems and launch ransomware. Timely updates close those entry points.
recommendation: Set and follow time limits for installing security updates, giving urgent fixes priority.

text: Does your organisation keep an up-to-date list of its devices and installed software?
why: Forgotten devices and software can miss updates and protection. A current list helps you find gaps before attackers do.
recommendation: Maintain a list of devices and installed software and update it whenever equipment or software changes.

text: Does your organisation regularly check its systems with a security scanning tool to find known weaknesses?
why: Security scans can reveal missing fixes and unsafe settings that ransomware attackers may exploit.
recommendation: Arrange regular vulnerability scans of your systems and assign someone to address the findings.

text: Does your organisation remove software that no longer receives security updates or keep it isolated from the internet and other systems?
why: Unsupported software can leave weaknesses that will not be fixed. Isolation limits attackers' ability to reach or spread from it.
recommendation: Replace unsupported software or isolate it from the internet and other systems until it can be replaced.

text: Does your organisation filter incoming email to block spam and messages that try to trick staff into sharing passwords or opening harmful content?
why: Deceptive emails can deliver ransomware or steal the account details used to launch an attack.
recommendation: Enable spam and phishing filtering for every work email account and keep the filtering settings up to date.

text: Does your organisation block dangerous email attachments and prevent files from the internet from running built-in commands called macros?
why: Harmful attachments and document macros can run instructions that install ransomware when a file is opened.
recommendation: Configure email and document settings to block dangerous attachment types and macros in files from the internet.

text: Does your organisation use a web filter to stop staff devices from connecting to known harmful websites?
why: Harmful websites can steal passwords or deliver ransomware. Web filtering can stop some of these connections before harm occurs.
recommendation: Enable web or website-address filtering on staff devices to block known harmful sites.

text: Are all remote desktop connections to your organisation's computers either disabled or protected behind a secure access gateway, rather than directly reachable from the internet?
why: Attackers look for exposed remote desktop connections to break into computers and deploy ransomware.
recommendation: Disable unused remote desktop access and place any required connections behind a secure access gateway with a second identity check.

text: Does your organisation use a firewall that blocks network connections unless they have been explicitly allowed for work?
why: Blocking connections by default reduces the routes attackers can use to enter systems or spread ransomware.
recommendation: Configure the firewall to deny connections by default and allow only those needed for work.

text: Are your organisation's critical systems kept in separate network areas with access between areas limited to what is needed?
why: Separating network areas can limit how far ransomware spreads from an infected device.
recommendation: Separate critical systems from everyday devices and guest networks, allowing only necessary connections between them.

text: Are all your organisation's computers and servers protected by active, up-to-date security software that detects harmful programs?
why: Device protection can detect and stop harmful software before it damages files. Unprotected devices can provide a starting point for an attack.
recommendation: Install and maintain active antivirus or endpoint detection protection on every computer and server.

text: Are unused system services and outdated ways of sharing files or connecting devices disabled across your organisation?
why: Unneeded services and older connection methods can give attackers extra routes to enter systems or spread ransomware.
recommendation: Have your IT support disable unused services and outdated file-sharing or connection methods on devices and servers.

text: Does your organisation collect important system and security activity records in one central place for review?
why: Central records help connect warning signs across devices and investigate how a ransomware attack started.
recommendation: Collect important device, sign-in and security activity records in a central location with restricted access.

text: Does your organisation receive alerts for unusual activity, such as many files being renamed or changed very quickly?
why: Rapid changes to many files can be a sign of ransomware. An early alert can help you act before more data is affected.
recommendation: Set up alerts for unusual activity, including rapid changes or renaming of large numbers of files.

text: Does your organisation monitor repeated failed sign-ins and administrator activity outside normal working hours?
why: Repeated sign-in failures may signal an attempted break-in. Unexpected administrator activity can indicate that an attacker has gained powerful access.
recommendation: Monitor repeated failed sign-ins and administrator activity outside expected hours and investigate unusual patterns.

text: Does your organisation have a named person or team responsible for reviewing security alerts and arranging a response?
why: Alerts only help if someone acts on them. Clear responsibility reduces delays while ransomware spreads.
recommendation: Assign a person or team to review security alerts and arrange backup cover when they are unavailable.

text: Does your organisation have a written plan describing what to do during a ransomware attack and how to recover safely?
why: A written plan helps people act quickly under pressure and avoid decisions that could worsen an attack.
recommendation: Write a ransomware response plan covering containment, communication and safe recovery of essential services.

text: Does your organisation keep an up-to-date list of response roles and contacts, including who reports an incident to CERT-In in India and how to do so?
why: Clear roles and reachable contacts reduce confusion during an attack. A known reporting route helps the responsible person contact CERT-In promptly.
recommendation: Maintain a response contact and roles list that assigns CERT-In reporting and records the reporting steps from CERT-In's official website.

text: Does your organisation have agreed steps and authorised staff to quickly disconnect an infected device or system from the network?
why: Quickly isolating infected systems can limit ransomware spreading to shared files and other devices.
recommendation: Define who can isolate infected systems and document how to disconnect them quickly from wired and wireless networks.

text: Does your organisation practise its ransomware response through drills or discussion exercises and keep an offline copy of the plan?
why: Practice reveals gaps before a real attack. An offline copy keeps instructions available if systems are locked or disconnected.
recommendation: Schedule ransomware response exercises and keep an up-to-date offline copy of the plan where response staff can reach it.

text: Does your organisation give all staff regular training on safe email, passwords and recognising ransomware risks?
why: Staff who recognise common warning signs are better prepared to avoid actions that could let ransomware in.
recommendation: Provide security awareness training when staff join and repeat it regularly with practical ransomware examples.

text: Does your organisation run safe practice exercises using simulated deceptive emails and explain the warning signs afterwards?
why: Practice emails help staff learn to recognise phishing attempts before a real message leads to stolen passwords or ransomware.
recommendation: Run safe phishing simulations and follow them with supportive explanations of how to spot and report suspicious messages.

text: Does your organisation give staff a simple, clearly explained way to report suspicious emails quickly?
why: Quick reports let the organisation investigate a harmful message and warn others before more people open it.
recommendation: Provide one easy reporting route for suspicious emails and explain it to every staff member.

text: Does your organisation give IT support and administrator staff specific training on recognising ransomware warning signs and taking the first response steps?
why: Staff with system access need to recognise technical warning signs and act quickly to contain a possible ransomware attack.
recommendation: Train IT support and administrator staff to recognise ransomware signs and follow the organisation's containment and reporting steps.
